title: Ottoman in Latin letters
goal: Read Ottoman Turkish in transcription, put it into modern Turkish, and hear what an Ottoman word does in a modern sentence.

intro.text: Most Ottoman texts reach today's readers in Latin letters: a circumflex for a long vowel, an apostrophe for an Arabic consonant, a hyphen for the izafet. Read slowly, word by word, and look for each word's modern partner.

vocab.en: to simplify; to rewrite (an old text) in modern words
to honour with one's presence; (ironic) to deign to come
His or Her Excellency (now mostly ironic; zatıaliniz: Your Excellency)

exercises.title: Müselles ve üçgen
exercises.passage:
Elif üniversitede tarih okuyor ve bu dönem Osmanlıca dersi alıyor. Geçen hafta hocası, eski bir matematik kitabından alınmış bir cümleyi çeviri yazıyla tahtaya yazdı: “Bir müsellesin mesaha-i sathiyyesi, kaidesiyle irtifaının hâsıl-ı darbının nısfına müsavidir.”

Elif önce hiçbir şey anlamadı. Sonra kelimeleri tek tek sözlükte aradı: müselles üçgendi, kaide taban, irtifa yükseklik. Nısıf yarı, müsavi de eşit demekti. Birden cümle açıldı: bir üçgenin alanı, tabanı ile yüksekliğinin çarpımının yarısına eşitti!

Elif güldü: “Hocam, bunu ben ilkokulda öğrenmiştim.” Hoca da güldü: “Evet, ama dedelerimizin dedeleri aynı kuralı bu kelimelerle öğrendi. Kelimeler değişti, üçgen değişmedi.”

Dersin sonunda öğrenciler cümleyi sadeleştirdiler. Elif o akşam annesine telefon etti. Annesi şöyle dedi: “Senin büyük deden de hep mektep derdi.”
exercises.translation: Elif studies history at university and is taking an Ottoman Turkish class this term. Last week her teacher wrote on the board, in transcription, a sentence taken from an old maths book: 'Bir müsellesin mesaha-i sathiyyesi, kaidesiyle irtifaının hâsıl-ı darbının nısfına müsavidir.' At first Elif understood nothing. Then she looked the words up one by one: müselles was a triangle, kaide the base, irtifa the height. Nısıf meant half, and müsavi equal. Suddenly the sentence opened up: the area of a triangle was equal to half the product of its base and its height! Elif laughed: 'Sir, I learned this at primary school.' The teacher laughed too: 'Yes, but our grandparents' grandparents learned the same rule with these words. The words changed; the triangle didn't.' At the end of the class the students rewrote the sentence in modern Turkish. That evening Elif phoned her mother, who said: 'Your great-grandfather always said mektep too.'

questions.q: What did Elif do first to understand the sentence?
options: She looked the words up one by one

questions.q: What does the teacher mean by *Kelimeler değişti, üçgen değişmedi*?
options: The rule is the same; only the vocabulary changed
Triangles were different in Ottoman times

questions.q: Which sentence gives Elif's thought in the narrator's voice, as free indirect speech?
options: Birden cümle açıldı: bir üçgenin alanı, tabanı ile yüksekliğinin çarpımının yarısına eşitti!
questions.explain: Third person and past, but her own discovery and her exclamation, with no *diye düşündü* ([C2 unit 2](gp-free-indirect)).

exercises.text: Eski metinlerde ma'lûm diye yazılan kelimeyi bugün ___, mes'ele diye yazılanı da ___ diye yazıyoruz.
exercises.en: A word written ma'lûm in old texts we write … today, and one written mes'ele, …
exercises.hint: Modern spelling drops the apostrophe and, here, the circumflex.
exercises.explain: The apostrophes stood for the Arabic ayn and hemze, which Turkish doesn't pronounce; modern spelling writes *malum* and *mesele*.

exercises.question: In *Takvîm-i Vekâyi'*, the name of the first Ottoman gazette, what does the final apostrophe stand for?
options: The Arabic consonant ayn, which Turkish doesn't pronounce
A suffix that has been left out
The end of a proper name

why.1: Nothing is missing: the word ends in an Arabic consonant.
why.2: An apostrophe before a suffix on a name is modern spelling; here it belongs to the word.
why.3: Long vowels are marked with a circumflex, as in *Vekâyi*.

exercises.explain: In a simplified transcription, an apostrophe inside or at the end of a word stands for ayn or hemze: *san'at*, *mes'ele*, *Vekâyi'*.

accept: With your permission, let us end the meeting here.

With your permission let us finish the meeting [here|at this point|now]
With your permission let us close the meeting [here|at this point|now]
With your permission let us wrap up the meeting [here|at this point|now]
If I may let us [end|finish|close|wrap up] the meeting [here|at this point|now]
If you [will allow me|allow me|do not mind] let us [end|finish|close|wrap up] the meeting [here|at this point|now]
exercises.explain: *Müsaadenizle* is a polite, slightly formal **with your permission**; *izninizle* says the same with the everyday word.

exercises.question: Selin arrives an hour late to dinner with friends. Which remark is ironic?
options: Geç kaldın, bir şey mi oldu?

why.1: A friendly greeting with a real question: no irony.

exercises.explain: *Zatıalileri* (Her Excellency) and *teşrif etmek* (to honour with one's presence) are far too grand for a friend who is late: that is the joke.

exercises.prompt: In legal style: This contract has been signed today.

reject.why: Correct Turkish, but the task asks for legal style, and contracts open with *işbu*.
Correct Turkish, but the task asks for legal style, and contracts open with *işbu*.

exercises.hint: Legal Turkish has its own word for **this**, from this lesson's vocabulary.
exercises.explain: *İşbu* (this) belongs to contracts; `-mIştIr` is the formal past of documents ([C1 unit 2](gp-dir-general-truth)).

exercises.text: Duyuru: Kütüphanemiz ___ kapalıdır. Anlayışınız için teşekkür ederiz.
exercises.en: Notice: Our library is currently closed. Thank you for your understanding.
exercises.explain: *Hâlihazırda* (at present) is formal but current, at home in a notice. *Binaenaleyh* means **consequently**, and *zatıalileri* is a mock-grand title.
*Müsaade* ends in the front vowel e, so the possessive is *-niz* and *ile* becomes *-le*: *müsaade-niz-le*.

exercises.task: This sentence is written in the Ottoman style of the early 20th century. Rewrite it in today's Turkish (*sadeleştir*), replacing every Ottoman word that has a modern partner. Gloss: *netice* result.
